extraction.name: FLORES-101
extraction.description: An evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and professionally translated in 101 languages, with multilingual alignment and rich metadata to support machine translation evaluation and related tasks.
extraction.creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan
extraction.citeAs: Goyal, Naman, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, and Angela Fan. 2021. The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset construction consisted of three phases: sourcing sentences from English Wikipedia-related Wikimedia sources, designing and running pilot experiments to determine translation and quality assurance processes, and launching the translation workflow for over 100 languages. Source sentences were extracted from Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage. Article selection was random, followed by manual selection of typically 3 to 5 contiguous sentences while avoiding very short or malformed sentences. One paragraph per document was selected from the beginning, middle, or end, balanced across the corpus. Sentences were then translated by professional translators through a controlled workflow involving translation, editing, automatic quality checks, human evaluation by an independent language service provider, and re-translation when needed.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Others
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: All source sentences were extracted from multiple Wikimedia sources. Specifically, the English source sentences were collected from Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage, and were sampled from English Wikipedia-related content. The dataset also includes metadata such as Wikipedia URL, topic, and boolean flags indicating whether the sentence contained linked entities and images.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The sentence selection process involved selecting an article at random from each source and manually selecting a few contiguous sentences, avoiding malformed or very short segments. To avoid bias from document structure, one paragraph per document was selected from the beginning, middle, or end, with balanced distribution across the corpus. The dataset was divided into dev, devtest, and test splits. For translation collection, translations could go through multiple rounds of re-translation based on automatic checks and human evaluation until quality thresholds were met.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: After translation, the data underwent automated quality control checks including language identification, checking whether the translation copied the source sentence, checking for significantly different length, checking fluency with a language model, and checking whether the translation copied outputs from publicly available translation engines. If any checks failed, the language service provider had to re-translate until all verification was passed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Manual labeling and translation were used. Ten annotators in the lab selected source sentences and manually labeled all sentences by one of 10 sub-topics: crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, and travel. For the multilingual dataset, professional translators translated the source sentences into 101 languages. Within each language service provider, translated sentences were edited by different translators. An independent evaluation language service provider then performed human quality assessment, identifying error categories such as grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition or omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register, each with severity levels of minor, major, or critical.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed through a Translation Quality Score on a 0 to 100 scale, determined from the number and severity of identified errors. The acceptable threshold was set to 90%. Evaluators were encouraged to pay particular attention to unnatural translation errors. If the score was below the accepted threshold, translations and assessment reports were sent back for re-translation, and in some cases re-evaluated by humans. The paper also analyzes translation errors and reports that mistranslation was the largest error category across languages.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators in the authors' lab: 6 male and 4 female; with roles including researchers (scientists and engineers) and program/project managers; originally coming from East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Language identification tools, a language model for fluency checking, and sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU based heuristics for detecting likely copies from commercial translation engines were used as automatic checks.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dev and devtest sets are publicly downloadable, while the test set will not be released and will instead be available via a publicly available evaluation server. The primary motivation is to guarantee equivalent assessment of models and reduce overfitting to the test set. The authors also state that they hope to continue to expand the number of languages covered in FLORES-101 and make the test set available to various community efforts.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotator gender and region of origin were described for the sentence selection annotators.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: By publicly releasing a high-quality and high-coverage dataset, the authors hope to foster progress in the machine translation community and beyond. The paper states that many low-resource languages are spoken by the majority of the world's population and that improvements in translation quality would benefit speakers of these languages. The dataset is intended to support evaluation of regionally relevant language pairs such as Xhosa-Zulu, Vietnamese-Thai, and Spanish-Aymara.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses possible bias from document structure and addresses it by balancing paragraph selection across the beginning, middle, and end of articles. It also discusses the caveat that source sentences not in English are produced by human translators, raising the issue of translationese, though the authors conjecture these effects are marginal in low-resource evaluation. The authors also sought to reduce bias from popular translation engines by detecting and rejecting professional translations likely copied from commercial systems.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset sources all sentences from English Wikipedia-related sources rather than from many source languages, with the caveat that non-English source sentences in many-to-many evaluation are human translations and may exhibit translationese. The paper also notes that several languages considered beyond the final 101 were unable to meet the quality bar after rounds of re-translation. The test set is not publicly released to avoid overfitting and because releasing source sentences would also release target sentences in a many-to-many setting.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, including many-to-many multilingual translation systems. It supports dev, devtest, and test usage: the dev set is meant for hyper-parameter tuning, devtest for testing during development, and test for evaluation through a public server. The paper also states that the dataset can support document-level translation, multimodal translation, text classification, sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation.
